html:
The Battle of Cannae was fought on 2 August 216 BCE near the village of Cannae in Apulia, southeast Italy. Hannibal's army surrounded and almost wiped out a much larger Roman army, in one of the worst defeats Rome ever suffered.

After Lake Trasimene, Rome raised the largest army in its history, under the consuls Paullus and Varro, to crush Hannibal. He let them attack. His centre, of Gauls and Spaniards, bent back slowly before the Roman push. Then his African infantry on both sides turned inward, and his cavalry, having beaten the Roman horse, closed the ring from behind. Packed together, the Romans could barely fight. Tens of thousands died, among them Paullus and many senators.

Much of southern Italy, including Capua, went over to Hannibal, and Philip V of Macedon made an alliance with him. But Rome refused to talk peace, raised new legions and passed emergency laws such as the Lex Oppia. The young Scipio was among the survivors. Cannae became the model of a battle of encirclement, studied by generals into the 20th century, and a turning point in the Second Punic War.
